name: mail-parser (Rust e-mail parser)
baseline: GMime 3.2.15, VMime (commit 5b01911), libEtPan! 1.10.1 and Dovecot 2.4.5 lib-mail (all C or C++, built with -O3 and called through C/C++ shims); the Rust mailparse 0.17.0 crate is also measured
workload: Parse RFC 5322/MIME e-mail messages (one message per call) in three workloads: full (parse and read every decoded leaf body with charset conversion to UTF-8), headers (decoded Subject, first From address, Date, Message-ID) and structure (content type of every MIME part), over eleven corpora (3,292 messages, 17.8 MiB: test suite, Enron sample, large attachments, newsletters, long header blocks, forwarded messages, 1 MB plain text).
claimed_speedup: README, geometric mean over the corpora (range): full workload 31x GMime (13 to 177), 20x VMime (7.8 to 80), 15x libEtPan! (5.7 to 69), 9.3x Dovecot (4.4 to 24), 3.0x mailparse; headers workload 14x GMime, 33x VMime, 19x libEtPan!, 5.2x Dovecot; structure workload 14x GMime, 31x VMime, 17x libEtPan!, 3.9x Dovecot. Example throughput, full workload, Enron 3,000 messages: mail-parser 2,420 MiB/s vs GMime 65, VMime 70, libEtPan! 96, Dovecot 366 MiB/s.
compiler_and_flags: Rust side: rustc 1.98.1, release profile (opt-level 3), mail-parser 0.11.9, criterion 0.8.2. C/C++ side (benches/compare/README.md): Apple clang 21; GMime configure with CFLAGS=-O3, VMime CMake Release with -O3 -DNDEBUG, libEtPan! built at -O3 (22 parser sources compiled directly), Dovecot configure with CFLAGS=-O3; shims compiled by build.rs at -O3 (-std=gnu11, -std=c++17). Library sources are pinned by SHA-256.
hardware: Apple M4 (Mac mini, macOS 26.6), median of three runs
why_faster: README feature list: SIMD kernels find boundaries and header fields (NEON on aarch64, AVX2 and SSE2 on x86-64), SIMD base64 and quoted-printable decoders (encodify), simdutf8 for UTF-8 validation, perfect hashing (hashify) for header names, charset labels and HTML entities, lazy decoding (bodies are not transfer-decoded or charset-converted until read) and zero-copy strings that borrow from the input.
stars_or_usage: 462 stars; parser inside Stalwart Mail Server
tradeoffs: Rust API; C++ callers need FFI. Bodies are decoded lazily, so the headers and structure workloads skip body work. Legacy CJK multi-byte charsets need the optional encoding_rs dependency. Does not build messages (separate mail-builder crate).
caveats: First-party harness, but it is a separate benches/compare crate with an equivalence check (results/check.md) that the README says confirms every library does the same work; I did not open check.md or summary.md. Measured on one machine (Apple M4, NEON path); the x86-64 AVX2 path is not measured. The C/C++ libraries are driven through shims written by the project and built without crypto, SSL and other optional features. Speed-ups include the effect of lazy decoding (the large-attachments corpus reaches 80,868 MiB/s in the headers workload because the bodies are never touched). The nearest competitor is the Rust mailparse crate, only 2.8x to 3.2x behind. No LTO or PGO setting is stated for either side. The wins over C libraries come from SIMD kernels and design (lazy, zero-copy), not from the language alone.

name: evtx (Rust Windows Event Log parser and evtx_dump)
baseline: libevtx evtxexport (C, libyal), built from source by the repo's benchmark script
workload: Convert a 30 MB Windows Security event log (samples/security_big_sample.evtx) to XML text written to /dev/null; wall-clock time measured with hyperfine (warmup 2, 5 runs by default in the script).
claimed_speedup: README table (30MB evtx, XML output): evtx 71.6 ms on 1 thread, 20.7 ms on 8 threads and 22.1 ms on 24 threads vs libevtx (C) 2.439 s, i.e. about 34x on one thread and about 118x on 8 threads (both derived from page data; the README gives no libevtx ratio itself). The README also states 'faster than any other implementation by order(s) of magnitude'.
compiler_and_flags: evtx 0.12.2: cargo release with profile-guided build (build_pgo.sh) and the fast-alloc feature (README); Cargo release profile and build_pgo.sh flags beyond that were not read. libevtx: scripts/bench_all_parsers.sh clones libyal/libevtx and runs ./configure --enable-static --disable-shared --enable-static-executables then make with no CFLAGS set (autoconf default, normally -g -O2; libevtx version not recorded).
hardware: 12-core AMD Ryzen 3900X, Arch Linux (Linux 7.0.11-arch1-1), bench commit 99a6def, run June 2026
why_faster: README credits a compiled-template rewrite (docs/compiled-templates.html, not opened), PGO and, for the 8-thread column, parallel chunk parsing. The one-thread gap over libevtx has no stated mechanism.
stars_or_usage: 966 stars; published as the evtx crate and PyPI wheel
tradeoffs: Read-only parser; CDATA nodes and EVTHandle nodes are unimplemented. Safe Rust with optional multithreading. Outputs XML or JSON.
caveats: Category fit is weak: the input is a binary log format and the output is XML text. The C baseline is the stock autoconf build (likely -O2, no PGO) while evtx is PGO-built, so the optimisation levels are not matched. The libevtx figure was carried over from a January 2026 run on the same machine while the evtx columns were re-measured in June 2026 after a rewrite. No check that evtxexport and evtx_dump emit equivalent XML was seen. First-party benchmark, one machine, one input file. The 8-thread column compares a parallel program against a single-threaded C tool.

name: ferrocat (Rust Gettext PO catalog engine)
baseline: GNU msgmerge (gettext-tools 1.0, C), run as a separate process per iteration
workload: Merge or update a 10,000-message Gettext PO catalog with freshly extracted messages, file to file (parse existing and new files, merge by exact identity, serialise).
claimed_speedup: README table (10k-message catalog, Apple M1 Ultra, median throughput): update with new strings 291 MiB/s vs msgmerge 4.8 MiB/s; full catalog update 150 MiB/s vs msgmerge 4.8 MiB/s; README text: 'roughly 31x ahead of GNU msgmerge'. From the checked-in report benchmark/results/gettext-workflows-ecosystem-v1-a84e6fb.json (10,000-message fixture, wall time per operation derived from page data): ferrocat update_catalog_file 16.7 ms vs msgmerge 415.6 ms (about 25x); ferrocat merge 7.9 ms vs msgmerge 418.1 ms (about 53x).
compiler_and_flags: Report records rustc 1.95.0-nightly (2026-01-29) and msgmerge (GNU gettext-tools) 1.0; Cargo profile and msgmerge build flags not stated.
hardware: Apple M1 Ultra, 64 GB RAM, macOS arm64 (report environment block)
why_faster: README: byte-oriented scanning and move-not-clone catalog paths in the merge; the update benchmark parses both files, merges and serialises.
tradeoffs: Rust-native API only (no first-party C or other host bindings); ICU MessageFormat and FCL catalog modes go beyond what msgmerge does.
caveats: First-party benchmark with checked-in JSON reports (one machine). The comparison is asymmetric: in the report ferrocat runs as a library call repeated 15 to 31 times inside one sample, while msgmerge is a spawned process (including process start-up and locale set-up) once per iteration, so the MiB/s columns reflect different work per timed unit (bytes processed per sample differ by an order of magnitude). msgmerge is a general GNU tool with fuzzy matching; ferrocat merges by exact identity only (README: 'merges by exact identity'). The README 31x and my derived 25x/53x differ because they normalise differently. Stars: 0, so the project is unproven in the field.

name: hist-rs (hist, Rust unique-line counter)
baseline: sort | uniq -c | sort -n built from the system sort and uniq (coreutils; GNU or BSD not stated, the run was on macOS)
workload: Count unique lines of a random 1M-line FASTQ-style file generated with nucgen (-n 1000000 -l 20), piped through each tool, timed with hyperfine (warmup 10); second benchmark deduplicates the stream (hist -u).
claimed_speedup: README table (MacBook M3 Pro): hist 231.5 ms vs naive 'sort | uniq -c | sort -n' 5637.6 ms (24.4x, derived from page data; repo description says 25x), vs the same pipe with LC_ALL=C 1219.5 ms (5.3x derived) and with LC_ALL=C plus -S 1G 1179.2 ms (5.1x derived), vs awk count pipeline 1265.4 ms (5.5x derived), vs uutils coreutils pipeline 890.1 ms (3.8x derived). Dedup mode: hist 180.6 ms vs awk '!seen[$0]++' 1307.1 ms (7.2x derived).
compiler_and_flags: Cargo.toml release profile: lto = true, codegen-units = 1; .cargo/config.toml: -C target-cpu=native; edition 2024; rustc version not stated. Baseline tool versions and flags not stated; exact commands are in the repo's justfile.
why_faster: Not stated in the README. Inference from Cargo.toml (hashbrown, bumpalo): hash-table counting over an arena instead of an O(n log n) sort of all lines.
tradeoffs: Holds every distinct line in memory (a hash table), so memory grows with the number of unique lines; output order is by abundance rather than the stable sort order of uniq.
caveats: Most of the headline 24x comes from the default-locale sort: with LC_ALL=C the gap shrinks to about 5x. The input is random 20-character sequences, so almost every line is unique, which is not typical for duplicate-heavy data. First-party, one machine, no baseline versions; sort and uniq on macOS are probably the BSD versions. The speedup is algorithmic (hash counting vs sorting), not a language-level effect. Sibling tools huniq and cuniq are already recorded separately.
found_via: Hacker News search-result snippet (a thread about replacing sort | uniq -c reported 25x throughput over coreutils with a hashmap tool, no title or link shown); the repo was then identified from the GitHub description '25x over sort | uniq -c' and opened (README, justfile, Cargo.toml, .cargo/config.toml).

name: xerg (xtreme-grep, Rust parallel grep)
baseline: system grep (implementation and version not stated; the test environment is macOS, so probably BSD grep)
workload: Search a large directory tree (a Rust target/ build directory with many files) for a pattern with grep and with xerg; also a single file and a small set of about 8 source files.
claimed_speedup: README: large dataset (target/ directory): system grep 28,122 ms vs xerg 1,590 ms (17.7x) and xerg -x 835 ms (33.7x); single file 4.0 ms vs 3.0 ms (25% faster); small multi-file set 3.0 ms vs 3.0 ms (parity, -x 4.0 ms is slower).
compiler_and_flags: 'Release builds' (README); no flags, no compiler version, no grep version.
hardware: 'macOS, multi-core system' (README); CPU model not stated
why_faster: README: parallel multi-core file scanning (CPU use about 484% to 745% vs about 96% for grep).
tradeoffs: PCRE-style regex rather than POSIX; different output format (pretty mode by default, -x for raw file:line:content); not a strict drop-in.
caveats: The win is parallelism: grep ran single-threaded over a directory while xerg used 5 to 7 cores, and the README concedes parity or slowdown on small inputs. Pattern, file set, grep version, hardware and number of runs are not stated, and the 28 s grep baseline probably also reads binary build artefacts. It is not compared against ripgrep, which does the same parallel work. Tiny project (3 stars). The speed-up is not attributable to the language.
found_via: Hacker News search snippets for ripgrep-inspired grep alternatives did not give a repo for this one; found through the crates.io API (query 'pcre', crate xerg 'Ultra-fast grep implementation in Rust'); opened the repository page, README and PERFORMANCE_ANALYSIS.md.

name: PDFOxide (pdf_oxide, Rust PDF text extraction)
baseline: MuPDF (via PyMuPDF) and PDFium (via pypdfium2), C and C++ PDF engines measured through their Python bindings
workload: Text extraction from 3,830 PDFs of the veraPDF, Mozilla pdf.js and DARPA SafeDocs corpora, single thread, 60 s timeout, no warm-up, mean and p99 time per document.
claimed_speedup: README Python table: PDFOxide 0.8 ms mean (p99 9 ms, 100% pass) vs PyMuPDF 4.6 ms (p99 28 ms, 99.3%) and pypdfium2 4.1 ms (p99 42 ms, 99.2%); README text: '5x faster than PyMuPDF'. Ratios 5.8x and 5.1x are derived from page data.
tradeoffs: Text and image extraction, PDF creation and editing; accuracy claims are 99.5% text parity with PyMuPDF and pypdfium2. MuPDF and PDFium also render pages, which this tool does not.
caveats: Hardware, compiler, flags and library versions are not stated; the baselines are Python wrappers, so per-call binding overhead is included on both sides (PDFOxide also measured through its Python binding). A bench/ and a benches/ folder exist in the repo but were not opened. Pass rate and extraction semantics differ by tool (empty or partial text counts as a pass in some harnesses), so the time per document may cover different work. First-party claim.
